  • The cliché of bad drip coffee from a cheap piece of plastic doesn’t apply anymore.
  • Our writers and editors have tested more than three dozen coffee makers over the years, and below we get into the ones that make a good cup of coffee, the ones that make a great cup of coffee, and the unfortunate ones that just can’t keep up with today’s coffee-brewing arms race.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ever since Starbucks started co-opting seemingly every street corner and strip mall and multiple waves of coffee snobbery (laudatory) have risen in direct opposition to mass market espresso, it’s safe to say the average consumer has changed what they expect from a cup of coffee. Just look at the coffee maker aisle in any big-box store and, along with single-serve and pod machines and other barista-replacing gadgets, you’ll find a slew of coffee makers that promise to make you dozens of drink styles, froth up some milk, and bring you “instant” cold brew. But sometimes the simplest way to make coffee is still pretty darn good. What we’re saying is don’t discount the drip coffee machine.

The cliché of bad drip coffee from a cheap piece of plastic doesn’t apply anymore. And even lots of cheap coffee makers are so much better than they used to be. If you’re in the market for a lot of coffee with little effort, your options are now legion. Companies like Breville, Fellow, Oxo, and Ratio have joined the original king of drip, Technivorm, in making quality appliances that better control factors like water temperature, flow rate, and bloom time, several of which brew coffee that’s almost as good as what you can get with a kettle and a pour-over setup.

Our writers and editors have tested more than three dozen coffee makers over the years, and below we get into the ones that make a good cup of coffee, the ones that make a great cup of coffee, and the unfortunate ones that just can’t keep up with today’s coffee-brewing arms race.

Recent findings suggest that new in this upgrade: We tested two new coffee makers with plastic-free brewing systems from Caraway and Simply Good Coffee. We also tested the new Braun OptiBrew Pro, which includes an onboard milk frother among other features.

Capacity: 10 cupsCarafe style: ThermalDimensions: 8.9" x 8.9" x 12"Weight: 9.6 lb.Features: Adjustable brew water ratio; adjustable temperature settings, flavor profile settings, programmable 24-hour timer; Wi-Fi connectivity; cold-brew capable; SCA Golden Cup capabilitiesWarranty: 3 years.

Sources indicate that fellow has a knack for making coffee gear that’s both beautiful and effective, and its automatic brewer fits right in. The Aiden is as close to a perfect drip coffee maker as we’ve tested because its designers considered nearly every need. It offers brew profiles with different water temperatures and times for light, medium, and dark roasts, and it tells you exactly how much coffee to use in both grams and tablespoons.

Recent findings suggest that but even with all its bells and whistles, the Aiden still has to make coffee that tastes good. And it does. Senior editor Noah Kaufman compared it side-by-side to carafes of pour-over and found both hit fruity and caramel notes, with real nuance and depth of flavor.

According to recent reports, what we love: The Aiden is customizable across so many parameters you might lose track: You can set water temperature (anywhere between 122°F and 210°F); the time and number of pulses of water (think of them as the individual water pours if you were making pour-over coffee); and bloom time that helps get rid of gasses that can make your coffee taste sour. This machine can also make a smooth pot of cold brew by slowly dripping water over the course of several hours. (Machines that claim they can make cold brew in minutes don't usually live up to their own hype.).

That sounds like a lot, but the Aiden is surprisingly easy to use thanks to a simple dial, a clear LCD screen, and straightforward instructions. And even though you can tweak your coffee in all the ways outlined above, you can also just use the Aiden like a basic one-button drip coffee maker. The Instant Brew option will use however much water is in the tank, brewing at water temperatures recommended by the Specialty Coffee Association (SCA) in its Golden Cup standards, which mark water temperature and coffee-to-water ratios for ideal flavor. To paraphrase Fellow’s founder, who visited us in the Test Kitchen, he wanted the machine to work for both coffee connoisseurs and total noobs.

According to recent reports, the Aiden also features a slew of carefully considered, where-have-you-been-my-whole-life details. Its two filter baskets—one for three cups or fewer and one for more than three cups—have spring-loaded seals to prevent drips when you remove them to empty the grounds into the garbage. It doesn't have a warming plate because it doesn't need one—the included thermal carafe kept coffee hot on the dining room table for around two hours. And the removable side water tank is easier to fill than either a built-in tank or one on the backside of the machine.

Recent findings suggest that during the testing, we also tried Fellow’s Drops program. It’s not exactly a coffee subscription—you order via text on demand—but it gives you access to various rare and small-batch beans from Fellow’s roaster partners. The Aiden comes preloaded with specific brew settings for recent Drops offerings, adjusting water temps and pulse cycles beyond the standard light/medium/dark profiles and the resulting coffee produced using the Drops settings was truly excellent. Brewing the same beans with both the Drops settings and the regular settings make a real difference. It’s one of the closest ways to recreate that “rare pour-over at your favorite café” experience at home.

Check out an even more detailed rundown on the Aiden here.

According to recent reports, what we’d leave: Compared to most of the drip coffee makers you’ll find at a major-box store, it’s somewhat expensive. However, within the recent wave of better-quality drip coffee machines, it falls right in line with average pricing we’ve come to expect from a daily coffee workhorse that produces this level of coffee.

In the long run: Noah has used the Aiden about five times a week for over two years, and it has lived up to its early promise. The coffee has remained consistently good, and we’ve had no problems with the interface, plus the removable side water tank has continued to prove its convenience.

Industry observers note that the Aiden is a precision machine, and regular maintenance matters. Noah found this out the hard way after too many months of skipping descaling, which eventually produced a loud noise that sounded like the pump might be on its last legs. To get an unfiltered read on customer service, he reached out as a regular customer rather than identifying himself as a Bon Appétit editor. Fellow responded within two days, pointed him toward descaling as a fix, and after he sent a video of the machine in action, offered to replace it entirely. They also recommended descaling monthly going forward, which felt a little aggressive, but the clear instructions were appreciated.

Capacity: 8 cupsCarafe-style: Thermal Dimensions: 13" x 6.5" x 14.25" Weight: 8 lb. Features: Blooms coffee, SCA Golden Cup capabilitiesWarranty: 5 years.

Ratio has been trying to limit the plastic across its whole lineup and offers up this stainless steel dripper as an add-on to the Ratio 6, which ensures no hot water or coffee touch plastic during the brewing process.

Industry observers note that the Fellow Aiden is a great coffee maker, but it has a lot going on. We know that some people’s ideal drip coffee maker is one you load up with coffee, turn on, and leave to do its thing. The Ratio Six (which is actually an 8-cup coffee maker, don’t let the name fool you) lets you do just that without compromising on the quality of the brew.

Sources indicate that what we love: It’s got one button that begins the brew process. There is no water temperature to set, no flavor profiles to adjust. But the brewing process, like the Fellow's, is designed to mimic a pour-over. The Ratio first blooms the coffee, then it uses a slower flow to improve extraction. The resulting coffee is absolutely delicious and takes no effort on your part. The Ratio Six (Series 2) includes a thermal carafe that outperformed all the others we tried (the Fellow was a close second), keeping coffee hot for over two hours.

What we'd leave: The Ratio's fixed water tank at the back of the appliance is a real bear to fill. We either had to set the machine sideways on the counter or slide it out from under a cabinet to fill it with water. The brew basket also sits on top of the carafe instead of being attached to the body in any way. That made it easy to empty, but it was a little precarious to set up until we got the hang of it.

In the long run: Ratio’s 5-year warranty is longer than just about any other coffee maker you can buy (Technivorm’s Moccamaster is the only other one with a warranty that long), and it’s clear why the organization felt comfortable making such a long offer. This thing has turned out to be as reliable a small appliance as we’ve ever used. It makes the same quality coffee more than a year later than it did the day we unboxed it.

Industry observers note that however, the things we found a little irritating about the Ratio’s design at the beginning did not get less irritating over time though. Unless it is set in an open space (i.e., not under a cabinet), filling the tank with water is cumbersome. And the small opening of the carafe demands a brush to properly clean it, which is not a deal breaker, but is a little annoying (especially compared to the wide opening of the Aiden’s carafe).

None of that takes away from the fact that, as far as small appliances go, this is as close to a buy-it-for-life pick as you’re going to find.

The Ratio was one of a small handful of machines we could really see working in the process.

A note on the wave of plastic-free coffee makers hitting the market: They’re not necessarily plastic-free. Countertop appliances are full of plastics, from their outer shells to their inner mechanisms because plastic parts are cheap, easy to mass produce, and, for many applications, durable enough. But a new(ish) crop of brewers eliminated plastic anywhere water travels through the machine in an attempt to avoid any possibility of plastic leeching into the coffee.

Aside from the Ratio Eight (below), which has featured a plastic-free brew path since it was introduced over a decade ago, our social media feeds have been serving us ads for newer plastic-free brew path models from Simply Good Coffee and Caraway, both of which we tested in our most recent update to this article.

According to recent reports, how much does plastic in the brew path matter? As with coating technology on nonstick pans, the science is developing. On a more subjective level, many coffee drinkers do say glass and steel brewing—along with the ceramic used in pour-over—tastes better.

Capacity: 10 cupsCarafe-style: GlassDimensions: 13" W x 6" D x 14" HWeight: 13 lb.Features: Plastic-free brew path, warming plate, insulated stainless-steel basket, reusable filter, quiet operation, cleaning modeWarranty: 2 years.

Everything hot (and cold) water touches in this machine is either stainless steel or glass, including the embedded reservoir. Caraway also remains committed to cute colors and stylish aesthetic, as the new coffee maker’s four available colorways are matched to those in existing Caraway products.

Industry observers note that what we love: The Caraway 10-cup coffee maker is a simple setup, so there's not much to dislike. It has single push-button operation and brews between 195°F–205°F meeting Golden Cup Standards with an automatically programmed bloom cycle. The stainless-steel reusable filter (you can also use paper if you wish) does a sufficient job of keeping silt out of our cup while also brewing rich, flavorful coffee, and the insulated basket means little heat is lost while the blooming occurs. Speaking of the basket, Caraway designed it to fit in two perpendicular directions, meaning you can orient the machine with the short side facing out, perhaps nestled between two other appliances, or with the long side pushed back wider against the wall.

Even though it costs more than either of the two coffee makers recommended above, it is quite a bit less expensive than the Ratio Eight, which is why we’re choosing to recommend it here instead. From a pure coffee perspective we prefer the Ratio, but we don’t love its $700 price tag. The Caraway makes consistently good coffee with its plastic-free arrangement for $200 less.

Industry observers note that what we’d leave: Considering the engineering it takes to produce a plastic-free brew path, we were left somewhat baffled by the lack of thought that seemed to go into the metal lid for the water reservoir, which just sort of sits on top—and loosely at that. The opening of the reservoir is nicely sloped so even a few errant drips will channel in. But the lid, which sits proud of the top surface of the unit and only slightly inset, can come dislodged just by shifting the machine (which you’ll need to do to fill it if it’s under a cabinet) or brushing your arm or hand across it too closely. Access to the reservoir is a bit limited as well, and while a water-only cycle is recommended weekly, plus a descaling for monthly maintenance, we’re a bit concerned about the prospect of something gunky getting in there and not being able to clean it out. Finally, there’s no option to preprogram the machine to brew automatically in the morning.

Capacity: 12 cupsCarafe-style: ThermalDimensions: 15" x 10" x 17"Features: Single-serve and half-carafe option, programmable timerWarranty: 2 years.

Industry observers note that we don’t have any real concerns with the quality of the coffee or the functionality of either the Fellow or Ratio coffee machines, but neither of them count as XL coffee makers. The Oxo 12-cup machine gives you 20% more volume while still keeping the quality of the coffee very high. It uses a rainmaker shower head to evenly saturate the grounds, and the resulting coffee is the kind of nuanced, fresh-tasting carafe we’d expect from something at this price point. There are a couple other features that push this one to the top of the pile.

According to recent reports, what we love: First is its range. It can brew anywhere from a single cup of coffee all the way up to 12 cups with no sacrifice on flavor or aroma. (Entertainers, take note: This means you can use the same machine to fuel both your normal weekday mornings and the occasional group brunch.) The Oxo also comes with a well-insulated stainless steel carafe that keeps coffee warm enough to drink for almost two hours and has an intuitive digital interface with a dial and a brew button that make it easy to schedule your coffee ahead of when you'll need it.

This coffee maker also has plenty of the little design touches that define Oxo products, including a removable shower head for easy cleaning and filter holders that are flat on the bottom so you can set them on the counter or in the sink after a brew without them spilling everywhere.

What we’d leave: The water tank is built into the body of the machine, and while the opening isn’t too small, it’s still not as easy to fill as a removable reservoir.

Braun BrewSense 12-Cup Drip Coffeemaker.

Capacity: 12 cupsCarafe-style: GlassDimensions: 7.9" x 7.9" x 14.2"Features: 1–4 cup options, adjustable brew strength, programmable timer, water filter, adjustable hot plate temperatureWarranty: 3 years.

It has been revealed that let’s get something straight about budget coffee makers: they don’t produce coffee on the same level as machines that precisely regulate water temperature and flow rate. These are the kind you might find at an adequate but not exceptional Airbnb. So we didn’t judge the Braun against the Fellow or the Ratio, but rather against the Mr. Coffees, Ninjas, and Black & Deckers of the world. By that measure, it did an admirable job. For a machine you can sometimes find on sale for $80, the coffee came out bright rather than stale or watery.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: There are a few ways you can tell a good cheap coffee maker from a bad one. One, it will produce water hot enough to actually extract flavor from ground coffee. When we measured the temperature of water as it ran through the Braun, it was more than 10℉ hotter than many of the other cheap coffee makers we tried. Another is that it will evenly distribute water over the coffee. Even if a coffee maker looks like it has a shower head that can spread water across the coffee bed, you still might end up with a machine that creates deep channels. Basically, a situation where streams of water get drilled through narrow areas of coffee. When we looked at the coffee bed of the BrewSense after making a pot, the coffee was evenly wet.

The proof will always be in the taste of the coffee, though, and the BrewSense pulled out many of the flavor notes we got from the Fellow and Ratio, though in a more muted way.

Also, for such an inexpensive coffee maker, the BrewSense came with some nice features, like the ability to slow down the water flow in order to brew small batches and a hot plate with adjustable temperatures to keep coffee from getting burnt while it sits.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: The glass carafe wasn’t our favorite. It flipped open a little too easily, which seemed like it could cause spills. And, frankly, a thermal carafe would have been nice. Some other budget machines have them.

EC-DAC50 Zutto 5-Cup Drip Coffeemaker.

Capacity: 5 cupsCarafe-style: GlassDimensions: 9" x 6" x 10.75"Features: Hot plate, removable water tankWarranty: 2 years.

Industry observers note that what we love: This little thing? Makes good coffee? Grading on an appropriate curve for something that costs less than $100, it absolutely does. Its design is unlike any other machine we tested, with a brewing cone that sits inside the carafe. That’s one way to achieve a small footprint. But it also keeps the coffee closer to the shower head, which helps maintain a hotter temperature than it otherwise might.

The coffee is not what you will get if you brew with the Fellow or the Ratio, but it can produce a more flavorful pot than any other sub-$100 machine we used (the Braun above is sometimes less than $100, but retails for more). And because it comes from well-respected Japanese brand, Zojirushi, the name behind our forever-favorite rice cookers and coffee tumblers, we trust it’s as high quality as something in this price range can get.

It also has a removable water tank that makes filling it each morning a much less irritating task, and is rare in cheap coffee makers.

What we’d leave: This is a small machine, only five cups. That may not be enough even in a two-coffee-drinker household if those two people need much more than eight ounces of coffee apiece. It also only has a single switch, which, on the one hand, makes brewing coffee easy (flip switch, brew coffee), but can lead to a bit of confusion. That switch also adjusts the temperature of the hot plate, but that isn’t made clear either on the machine or in the instructions. Zojirushi has famously dense instruction manuals that can be hard to follow, and that’s true even for something as simple as this.

In short, we made copious amounts of coffee in these machines. To keep the brewing process as consistent as possible, we used the same beans or grounds from the same roaster in each test—usually a blend of Counter Culture coffee beans, freshly ground with a Fellow Ode burr grinder. If the coffee maker came with a reusable filter, we used that; otherwise, we used standard Melitta paper filters.

If machines had features like a “bold” setting or the ability to brew half batches or single cups, we tested them to see what kind of difference the setting made (this was a particularly involved test with the Fellow and the Breville machines).

For machines with thermal carafes, we used probe thermometers to test how long they kept coffee above 110℉.

The single most notable thing you want from a drip coffee maker is a pot of coffee you actually want to drink. We looked for coffee makers that provided the most depth of flavor and nuance to their coffee. We discounted anything that made coffee that was burnt or watery.

Industry observers note that the point of a drip machine is to deliver your morning coffee in large quantities with minimal thinking from you. That means it should be easy to fill and easy to operate. If a machine has lots of customizable options like the Fellow Aiden, using them should still be straightforward enough that we could pick up their operation quickly.

Do they have special features, and do those features work?

A number of machines offered the ability to precisely regulate temperature. Some came with thermal carafes. Most had the very basic, but very important ability to schedule a brew ahead of time. We used every single option available.

Sources indicate that how do they look? How do they feel?

According to recent reports, as drip coffee makers have advanced technologically, they have also advanced aesthetically. We tested a number of machines that looked quite handsome on the countertop. We also noticed that a lot of the inexpensive machines felt too light and flimsy, which we’d consider an indicator that they may not last very long.

These machines, which include several of the fancier SCA-certified brewers as well as a number of simple, cheap ones, didn't make the short list of top picks, but they did well enough that we think you'll be happy if you pick one up.

Moccamaster KBGV 10-Cup Coffee Maker.

Recent findings suggest that A longtime darling of both online coffee publications and coffee lovers, Technivorm Moccamaster machines were some of the first to stake a claim on good drip coffee. They were actually the first to receive the SCA Golden Cup standard stamp of approval. And indeed, the coffee from the Moccamaster is tasty. It’s also simple in the way you’d traditionally expect a drip coffee maker to be. Just an on-off switch and a full pot–half pot switch.

Despite those two very major pluses, there are a few things that land the Moccamaster down here instead of up with our top picks. One is its look. Compared to the Ratio machine, which is just as simple but also offers extras like bloom time in the brewing process and a thermal carafe, the Technivorm takes up more counter space and doesn’t look nearly as sleek. But if you’re into the Technivorm’s diner coffee maker aesthetic (and I totally respect it if that’s your thing) it is a high-quality, long-lasting coffee maker (the Test Kitchen has had the same one for more than four years).

Ratio Eight Series 2 Coffee Maker.

Sources indicate that an OG in the plastic-free brew path drip coffee space, the only problem with the upcoming Ratio Eight is that it’s pretty damn expensive. But it’s also part coffee maker, part art object—with wood accents and a hand-blown glass carafe—so for the right person, the price may well be worth it. The coffee it brews is superb: evenly bloomed, well-extracted, and just as easy to make as with the Ratio Six thanks to the same single-button operation.

The latest version of the Ratio Eight adds a half-carafe mode (just long-press the brew button) that adjusts bloom time and flow depending on the batch size. It also comes with the thermal carafe to end all thermal carafes; it’s one of the heaviest we’ve ever used and kept water above 120°F for four hours.

Recent findings suggest that beautiful, functional, and built to last, this is a great machine. But with a price around $700, it’s in that echelon of luxury goods that isn’t accessible to a wide enough audience to make it a top pick.

8-Cup Coffee Maker with Podless Single-Serve.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to join the ranks of “better” drip coffee but don’t like the idea of spending $300 or more on your coffee maker, this mid-size, mid-priced machine from Oxo is a good choice. It gets water hot enough extract good flavor from ground coffee (we measured it at 196℉, which is on the low end of the acceptable range) and distributes it nicely thanks to Oxo’s showerhead design. It also blooms the coffee, though you might not know that if you don't read the fine print in the manual.

In a recent development, the Oxo has settings for a full 8-cup pot, a half pot, and a single cup. Oxo touts that single-serve capability as a major feature in its own description of the coffee maker, and it’s…fine. The individual cup didn’t brew up as flavorful as the full pot nor as flavorful as the single cups brewed by some other coffee makers, like the Fellow or Oxo’s higher-end 12-cup machine. But it does make good coffee, has a relatively small footprint, 7 inches wide and 10 inches deep, and feels well-built, as many Oxo products are. You can upgrade this coffee maker with a stainless-steel carafe which we didn’t test, but other Oxo insulated carafes performed well in our testing over the years.

OXO Brew 9 Cup Stainless Steel Coffee Maker.

Industry observers note that the Goldilocks size of the three Oxo coffee makers we tested ticks the main boxes for a high-end drip machine: It has good temperature control between 197℉ and 204℉, comes with a thermal carafe that keeps coffee warm for well over an hour, and it blooms the coffee. And like so many of Oxo’s products it comes with some subtle but smart design choices like keeping the lid of the grounds container attached to the machine, choosing a dial controller instead of a lineup of buttons, adding a freshness timer so you know how long the brewed coffee has been sitting, and a cleaning indicator to let you know when it’s time for descaling.

Sources indicate that on the flip side, the opening of the carafe is pretty narrow, so you’ll need to clean it with a bottle brush. Technically, this machine does not have the Golden Cup standard (though it does keep its water in the proper temperature range). It also offers fewer options than the Fellow, but isn’t as simple as the one-button Ratio.

Recent findings suggest that if you like the look of the Moccamaster but want something plastic-free (inside, at least), Simply Good Coffee’s The Brewer looks like a near-duplicate that comes in both a programmable and simpler on-off model. At nearly $400 for the latter, we think the similarly priced Caraway is a better plastic-eschewing choice. But it doesn’t let you set a brewing time, so if that’s important to you, then the programmable model at $40 more might be right for you. While it produced acceptable coffee overall, the parts felt a little flimsy at times with the reservoir lid not quite sitting flush or other pieces twisted slightly out of alignment out of the box. It takes #4 cone filters, like those used in pour-over setups, and one nice feature is that the filter basket sits flat on the counter or on a coffee scale, making measuring out grounds directly into the filter super easy. And there are gram ratios printed right on the reservoir to help you remember how to math when you’re still groggy. Lastly, one slightly confounding aspect is the inclusion of a Bloom switch, which must be turned on and, when engaged, produces markedly better tasting coffee. Which begs the question why not just have the “good coffee” mode be the only mode? “Very dark roasts and older, degassed beans benefit the most from skipping or heavily shortening the bloom phase,” Dean Rotchin, CEO of SimplyGoodCofee, told us. “While blooming is standard for fresh pour-over coffee to release trapped carbon dioxide (CO₂), certain roast profiles and conditions make it unnecessary or even counterproductive.” Lastly, this machine has a lot of parts (lids, filter holders, etc) which, generally, will just sit in their respective places most of the time, but if you have to this one in a cabinet, it can be a lot to keep track of.

Breville Luxe Drip Coffee Machine.

Seattle Coffee Gear (glass model).

Released in 2025, Breville’s Luxe Brewer has the look and feel of something designed specifically to compete in this world of increasingly customizable, increasingly high-end drip coffee makers. It offers the ability to set bloom volume, bloom time, water temperature, and flow rate. Plus, it makes cold brew overnight.

It has been revealed that this is a very good coffee maker, and once someone learns how to use it, they’ll be pleased with what they get. However, it costs almost the same amount as the Fellow Aiden, and it doesn’t give you quite as much. Bloom volume and flow rate, for example, can only be set to low, medium, and high. And while that might be plenty of optionality for most people in most situations, the point of having all these settings is to offer the ability to tease out exactly the flavor you want from any batch of beans. And we think the Fellow’s more precise capabilities are worth an extra 20 bucks.

It has been revealed that the interface of the Breville is also a little confusing. When you turn it on, it’s not immediately clear whether you’re adjusting settings or starting a brew cycle, and many of the customization options are represented by unlabeled icons. In an era of increasingly complex appliances, an intuitive, user-friendly interface is more vital than ever, and that’s where the Luxe Brewer falls short.

Zojirushi Dome Brew Classic Coffee Maker (Stainless Black).

In a recent development, with more than twice the capacity of the Zojirushi Zutto, the Dome offers a more traditional drip coffee maker experience. Like the Zutto, it produces coffee that punches above its weight for its price point, and the simplicity of a single switch that both brews coffee and turns on the warming plate. The removable showerhead does a nice job of fully saturating the coffee grounds, and a “bold” setting concentrates the water to extract bigger flavors. A standout design detail is its silicone gasket, which seals the top of the carafe during brewing to help keep the coffee at temperature as it drips through. If you’re looking for a straightforward, no-fuss machine that makes great coffee without breaking the bank, the Dome is an excellent pick.

Café Specialty Grind and Brew Coffee Maker.

Sources indicate that the Grind and Brew effectively toes the line between a simple, self-contained coffee maker and a techy, customizable one. The built-in grinder has six grind sizes and, while it’s not so nice or versatile that we’d pick it over a stand alone burr grinder, it gets the job done.

It has been revealed that this machine has variable temperatures between 185℉ and 205℉ and can brew using the SCA’s Golden Cup standard. That made its coffee both very good and very consistent. And it's a nice touch that you can easily switch between a setting for single cups and one for full carafes. Ultimately, it ended up in this middle space of not being able to do as much as the Fellow Aiden but holding a price tag that keeps it out of what we’d consider a “budget” range.

Café Specialty Drip Coffee Maker.

This is basically the Café Grind and Brew without the grinder or the single serve option, and the glass carafe model is actually priced low enough that we’d recommend it for someone who thinks the Fellow or the Ratio machines are a bridge too far for their wallet.

Recent findings suggest that like the Grind and Brew, you can use the SCA Golden Cup settings or customize water temperature between 185℉-205℉. Also like the Grind and Brew, the wide shower head evenly wets the coffee grounds and produces a high-quality pot. If you already have a solid coffee grinder or are willing to invest in one, this is a drip machine to consider.

GE Profile Smart Grind & Brew Coffee Maker.

According to recent reports, GE is the parent organization of Café, so it wasn’t surprising that some of the technology found in the Café Grind and Brew coffee maker used by the mother brand. The Profile features one significant improvement over the Café Grind and Brew: It shrank its countertop footprint. Instead of stretching out horizontally across the counter like the Café, the GE better integrates the water tank snugly into the back of the machine for a coffee maker that fits much more comfortably in a variety of kitchens.

Otherwise, it operates much like the Café. It allows for freshly ground single serve coffee, features an SCA Golden Cup setting, and has a user-friendly app that will get a fresh pot of coffee going from anywhere in the house. Like the Café version, we think the GE is good, but not great, and for just a little bit more money, you can get one of our top picks. After spending many months with both the Café and GE Grind and Brew models, we’ve found that the washable mesh filters let too many grounds wiggle their way into the coffee and regularly found sediment at the bottom of our cups.

Sources indicate that yet another machine that meets the Golden Cup standard (it’s become table stakes for “good” drip coffee makers at this point), the Zwilling Enfinigy makes coffee on par with the Café and Technivorm machines and is less expensive than all of them. Despite a high end look though, it’s also lighter weight, which makes it feel cheaper by comparison.

According to recent reports, it has a number of standard features: the ability to brew between 2 to 12 cups, a timer to proposal brews ahead, and a keep warm function. Like the Simply Good Coffee machine above it also offers the curious feature of a bloom function that you can toggle on and off. Blooming coffee seems like all upside and no downside, so we can’t think of a good reason you’d ever want to toggle it off. Maybe you like off flavors in your coffee?

Sources indicate that the Aarke machine is a beautiful, high-quality coffee machine, no doubt about it. It brews coffee with temperature control precise enough to earn it a rating from the Specialty Coffee Association and has a couple other nice features like a bloom function that you can toggle on or off by holding the single button on the machine. It's most effective when paired with Aarke's burr grinder, which can read how much water is in the dripper and grind coffee to match. You can read our review of the complete system here, but you don't need the grinder to make use of the brewer.

The issue with the Aarke is that it's not as customizable as the Fellow and, if you want a thermal carafe, will cost you quite a bit more than the Ratio Six. But if you're focused as much on aesthetics as you are on coffee, you might be ready to swallow the price bump.

Braun PureFlavor 14‑Cup Programmable Coffee Maker.

First the good: As programmable coffee makers under $100 go, they don’t come better than this Braun model, consistently priced below the Braun BrewSense we recommend up above. It can draw more flavor out of ground coffee than anything in this price range has business doing. The coffee bed revealed no channeling, meaning even water distribution and better extraction. The machine has an alarm setting so coffee will be ready when you wake up and has three different brew settings, including “bold” and over ice (which produced better iced coffee than some much more expensive machines).

So why does the Pureflavor miss out on a spot as the top budget pick? Because of a design you might actually like but we do not: It has a touchscreen. Unlike the BrewSense, which uses tactile buttons, the Pureflavor has a touchscreen interface. That’s not a problem in and of itself—some people like touchscreens, some don’t. It does raise durability concerns though. We’ve used enough touchscreen items in our product testing (and had enough fail) that seeing one at this price point makes us cautious about recommending it.

Calphalon Programmable 14-Cup Coffee Maker.

Industry observers note that the Calphalon’s coffee was just as good as what we got from my favorite Braun machine: rich, flavorful, more than we typically expect from a cheap coffee maker. It also had the same features, including the different settings for the hot plate. We thought the Braun’s interface was a little easier to use—all the buttons are clearly labeled and in one line as opposed to the Calphalon, which has a couple buttons that felt sort of hidden away at the top of the machine. And while prices on these coffee makers can bounce around a little bit, the Calphalon is typically a little bit more expensive than the Braun.

Mr. Coffee Stainless Steel 10 Cup Programmable Coffee Maker.

Mr. Coffee is sometimes used as shorthand for a cheap, meh coffee maker. But the brand has come a long way from the basic machine on your parents' or grandparents' counter growing up. This is still a very affordable machine, but comes with a thermal carafe that kept coffee warm for about an hour and a detachable water reservoir that makes it easy to fill without spilling. The coffee itself was on the watery side, but was still perfectly drinkable.

Kenmore 12-Cup Drip Coffee Maker.

According to recent reports, it comes with fewer features than either of the Braun coffee makers, but it produced coffee that ran close to them in terms of flavor. It has bold and 1-4 cup brew settings, making suitable for large or small coffee drinking households, and a simple interface that requires no explanation. It feels quite cheap—thin plastic and glass—but it also costs less than just about anything else we’ve tested, so in that way it meets expectations. If you’re looking for an alternative to the Zojirushi for some reason that’s just as inexpensive, you should be satisfied with this Kenmore.

Cuisinart Perfectemp 14-Cup Coffee. Maker With Glass Carafe.

According to recent reports, the big selling point of the Cuisinart Perfectemp is its size. It can brew 14 cups of coffee (that’s coffee-sized cups—five ounces, not eight ounces). It makes adequate tasting coffee, and the 1-4 cup setting, which adjusts the extraction time for less water, still produces flavorful results. We didn’t notice much difference when switching between regular and bold strength though. Ultimately, testers liked the flavor and the extra features of the Braun, which put it over the top here.

Even though some of the coffee makers on this list make coffee that’s tasty enough, they either lack the features, design, or value of the machines up above.

It has been revealed that braun’s OptiBrew Pro is trying to do a lot, and there are some aspects we loved, including smart water consumption from the reservoir (it only uses the amount for the desired cup or carafe size you select), sleek interface, and decent customization and programmability. However, among its many promises, it tries to masquerade as an espresso maker with “single shot” capability and an attached, foldaway milk frother. But the faux-spresso we got from it wasn’t satisfying enough to make us ditch our espresso machine. And wand-style milk frothers can be bought for under $10 and take up little space. We found the OptiBrew Pro’s operation a bit finicky, including the rear-mounted water tank and brew basket lid, which snapped closed and required a bit of effort to open. In other words, the lack of endorsement here does not come down to it being necessarily a bad coffee maker. Its added features just didn’t work well enough to justify paying more than you would for the BrewSense.

Ninja 12-Cup Programmable Brewer.

It has been revealed that as budget coffee goes, what I got from the Ninja was good, not great. It was a little more watery, and even on the “rich” setting tasted flatter than some machines’ regular coffee. The removable side water tank is a nice design touch, it’s easy to take off, refill, and replace. But there’s better cheap coffee out there.

According to recent reports, this is, to my knowledge, Mr. Coffee's first attempt to really play in the luxury coffee maker space. And retailing at $200 at the time of writing, it's definitely got the price tag to be there. In terms of performance the coffee was on par with lots of the mid-tier machines I tested—nuanced, sometimes fruity. It too uses SCA standards for its brewing.

Recent findings suggest that the thing that should justify the jump in price from say, the $150 Zwilling machine above, is the Mr Coffee’s ability to make quick cold brew in under 10 minutes. But I found the cold brew a little bit flat in flavor. Fine in a pinch, and if you didn’t want to go to the trouble of using a cold-brew coffee maker, but not what you’d expect from immersion cold brew. If you’re planning to spend in this price range, a number of the coffee makers above will serve you better. Do note that this Mr. Coffee also has tea and iced tea settings, which, while I didn’t consider them here, do make this a pretty versatile machine.

Recent findings suggest that this Mr. Coffee, unlike the more expensive models I tested, made passable coffee, but not anything I’d describe as tasty. It was a little on the watery side and there was some channeling in the coffee bed. The features were standard for a sub $100 coffee maker: a brew timer, a bold brew setting, and a 1–4 cup brew setting. Considering the competition here though, you’d have to grade on a pretty steep curve to give this one a passing mark.

The Bonavita One Touch has the same irritating problem of balancing the filter basket on top of the carafe that the Ratio machine does, but unlike the Ratio machine, it doesn’t brew coffee so good as to overcome that matter. The coffee tastes fine, the carafe holds in heat well for over an hour, and it’s super simple to use, but at this price point you can get something better from a Café machine or a refurbished Technivorm.

It has been revealed that despite being the biggest name in pour-over coffee, Chemex’s attempt to automate the process didn’t work out so well. Testers preferred the coffee from all of the Golden Cup machines to this one, which just didn’t have quite the nuance and depth of flavor. If you watch the machine work though, you’d assume it would. It allowed for a bloom period and the water flow started and stopped in a way that mimics making pour-over. The Ottomatic is compatible with 3-, 6-, and 8-cup Chemex carafes, though you can also get an included carafe with the machine.

Sources indicate that this machine comes with a thermal carafe, which is a nice addition for a budget coffee maker, but the coffee tasted weak. It has a couple extra features like a timer and a reusable filter. This is a machine you wouldn’t be upset to find at an Airbnb or at your in-laws house, but I wouldn’t encourage you to run out and buy it for yourself.

Amazon Basics 12-Cup Digital Coffee Maker.

According to recent reports, this is the cheapest coffee maker I tested and it shows. It comes with a delay timer to set a brew ahead of time, but that’s it. The coffee wasn’t undrinkable, but it certainly wasn’t memorable—a rather flavorless way to fill your body with caffeine in the morning. Because the difference in price between this and what I consider a nice budget coffee maker is only $30 or $40, I don’t think this one is worth it.

Black & Decker 12-Cup Coffee Maker.

In a recent development, despite trying quite a few inexpensive coffee makers, I didn’t have much really bad coffee, except from this machine. It tasted like dirt. And not in a “mmm, I like the earthy undertones of this bean blend” dirt. Like actual dirt. It comes with a thermal carafe, which is impressive for a machine that costs around $60 at the time of writing. But you may want to fill that thermal carafe with coffee from a different machine.

Melitta Vision 12-Cup Luxe Coffee Maker.

Recent findings suggest that let’s start with the good: The Melitta coffee maker is the only one I’ve seen that allows different configurations. The control panel rotates 270 degrees on the base of the machine so it can stretch across the counter from left to right (easier to fill with water) or back to front (a more compact footprint for smaller kitchens). It’s also a good-looking machine—matte white with gold and wood accents.

But unfortunately the coffee was so-so. Even on the bold setting it lacked much flavor. The top of the fixed water tank was a little sticky and annoying to fill. If it cost $100 this would be a reasonable budget machine, especially with its aesthetics, but with prices ranging from $140 to over $200 depending which retailer you go to and which color you choose, I think there are better choices out there.

Beautiful Programmable 14-Cup Coffee Maker.

In a recent development, drew Barrymore’s Walmart-only brand has produced a couple of hits in our product testing, most notably its stand mixer. Aesthetically, Drew’s drip coffee maker has the soft lines and color palate that could make it very appealing on the counter, and a set of features that usually cost 30% or 40% more, like a 1–4 cup brew setting and three variable brew strengths. But the coffee just didn’t have much flavor. It makes me think the heating element just can’t produce water that’s hot enough to properly extract the coffee. If price is the main driver of your coffee maker purchasing decision, it’s absolutely worth spending $35 or $40 more to get one of the Zojirushi coffee makers or the Braun Pureflavor.

Ninja Programmable XL 14-Cup Coffee Maker.

Like most of the coffee makers I don’t recommend here, the Ninja didn’t make terrible coffee, it made bland coffee. It has a few convenient features: A very small footprint considering its jumbo 14-cup capacity and a removable water tank that makes filling it in the morning easier than most coffee makers in this price range. But even coffee brewed with the “rich” setting tasted rather watery. There are a whole range of machines that brewed up better pots for the same cost or less, so I recommend you try one of those.

How do I make the best coffee with my drip coffee maker?

The flavor of your drink will largely depend on the coffee you’re using, the quality of the hot water you’re using (this really does make a difference), and the ratio of coffee to water.

It has been revealed that to make the best-tasting cup, always use freshly roasted, high-quality coffee beans at a medium grind size—buy whole beans and grind them right before you brew your coffee (here are our favorite coffee grinders). If you want to keep your beans fresher longer, keep them in a vacuum sealed container like this one.

It has been revealed that use filtered water; some drip coffee machines have a built-in water filter that will take care of this for you (just remember to change it out as directed). You’ll also want to use a scale to measure a coffee-to-water ratio of 1-to-16, or 16 grams of water for every gram of coffee. Start with this ratio, then feel free to play around and adjust according to your preference.

Specific brew temperature is also vital for proper flavor extraction so, if you can, go with a drip coffee maker that has precise temperature controls or at least an accurate thermostat that controls the temperature within a small window, like one our top picks..

What does it mean for a machine to be SCA certified?

Sources indicate that SCA stands for the Specialty Coffee Association. "SCA certified" is a technical designation, but the short version is this: The coffee maker can consistently brew a pot that meets a set of quality standards established by coffee pros. That includes maintaining a steady brewing temperature between 194°F and 204°F and achieving an even extraction of soluble compounds from the grounds.

Should you use those reusable, mesh filter baskets.

In terms of quality, we've found these mesh baskets generally produce worse coffee. The mesh, especially in the cheap coffee makers that usually use it, is frequently not fine enough to keep coffee solids out of the final product. If you have one, you can see this yourself by swishing around the last dregs of the carafe or your cup. You'll probably see a thin layer of coffee sludge on the bottom.

In a recent development, unbleached paper filters do a better job of producing clean coffee and, from a sustainability standpoint, are compostable. There's some debate about whether unbleached filters impact the flavor in problematic ways, but we've used them regularly and haven't noticed a large impact. For drip coffee makers both Melitta (used in this test) and If You Care make filters our editors use often.

Industry observers note that noah Kaufman: I’ve been helping leading product testing and reviews at Epicurious and Bon Appétit since 2021, during which time I’ve drowned myself in coffee, for both professional and personal reasons. In my kitchen I now have six different ways to brew it and a weekly influx of beans from roasters and regions all over the world.

Latest Update: A Brief Guide to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nike Sneaker Dupes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do.
  • Industry observers note that even the name is a joke.
  • The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do. We’d already spotted Air Force 1 dupes in the trailers, but now that we can finally play the long-awaited masterpiece itself, we’re taking a closer look at what else is on the shelves. There are tons of different sneaker stores sprinkled throughout the game, and Eris—Rockstar’s fictional answer to Nike—has given us a lot to work through.

Industry observers note that even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a big, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Off-White x Nike Air Max 97 ‘White’.

Some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

Recent findings suggest that arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

Air Jordan 1 High OG ‘Yin Yang’.

The Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

Recent findings suggest that there are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

It has been revealed that it gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

Sources indicate that we’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

A version of the story originally appeared on British GQ.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kate Middleton is sharing a deeply personal look at life after cancer.
  • “Cancer does change you,” Kate said.
  • Kate first publicly shared her cancer diagnosis in March 2024, revealing that doctors had discovered cancer following major abdominal surgery two months earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kate Middleton is sharing a deeply personal look at life after cancer. On Saturday, November 21, the Princess of Wales released the first trailer for Heal, a new documentary that will explore the emotional realities of a cancer diagnosis, recovery, and finding hope in the face of uncertainty.

“Cancer does change you,” Kate said. “It changes your body. It changes you physically. But tHere’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”.

Kate first publicly shared her cancer diagnosis in March 2024, revealing that doctors had discovered cancer following major abdominal surgery two months earlier. At the time, she remarked she was undergoing preventative chemotherapy and that she and Prince William had taken time to explain the news to their three children before making it public. In September 2024, she announced that she had completed chemotherapy, while emphasizing that her recovery was ongoing. “My path to healing and full recovery is long and I must continue to take each day as it comes,” she wrote. In January 2025, she confirmed that her cancer was in remission, but noted that adjusting to a “newly introduced normal” takes time. Later that July, during a hospital visit, she spoke candidly about the challenges of life after treatment, explaining that the period following chemotherapy can be “really, really difficult” as patients adjust to life outside the clinical care system.

The documentary follows the princess as she takes on the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales within 24 hours. Along the way, she reflects on her own experience and connects with others navigating serious illness. The trailer also offers glimpses of Kate embracing her children and husband, Prince William, as well as an emotional exchange with her younger brother, James Middleton.

“Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?” James asked Kate, referring to the tradition of ringing a bell to mark the end of cancer treatment.

“Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she responded.

“So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” he affirmed.

According to recent reports, through Heal, Kate hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery, and life beyond cancer. According to the documentary’s official announcement, the princess also hopes to help transform access to holistic cancer care that supports well-being, resilience, and quality of life during and after a diagnosis. All funds received through the documentary’s distribution will go to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which supports people living with and beyond cancer.

“Healing is a journey,” she states in the trailer. “How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”.

Here’s everything to know about Heal, including its release date and where to watch.

Recent findings suggest that heal explores the physical and emotional impact of serious illness, focusing on the ways people find comfort, strength, and hope during and after a cancer diagnosis. The film also highlights the importance of connection and holistic care, with Kate sharing her own reflections alongside conversations with others navigating illness.

Recent findings suggest that the documentary was produced by Will Warr’s Detail Films and directed by Benji Jackson. Its original score was composed by Erland Cooper.

It has been revealed that all funds received through the documentary's distribution will go to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity. Kate and Prince William became joint patrons of the hospital in January 2025, following her treatment there.

Heal will premiere in the United States on Monday, November 30, at 8 P.M. ET on NBC. It will also air on Bravo at 11:30 P.M. ET, with streaming available on Peacock beginning Tuesday, December 1.

In the United Kingdom, the documentary will be available on BBC iPlayer beginning at noon on Sunday, November 29, before airing on BBC One that evening. It will premiere in Australia on Channel 9 and 9Now on Tuesday, December 1, and in Canada on CTV and Noovo on Monday, December 7, with streaming on Crave beginning December 8.

It has been revealed that the first trailer for Heal was released on the Princess of Wales’s official Instagram account. Watch it below.

The Best Foods To Buy At Costco In November

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the holiday season is on the horizon, and Costco is celebrating with plenty of festive foods in every corner of the warehouse.
  • According to recent reports, I spend all year keeping tabs on the latest and greatest products to hit Costco shelves.
  • Here’s what’s available this November—there are some treats you don’t want to miss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the holiday season is on the horizon, and Costco is celebrating with plenty of festive foods in every corner of the warehouse. Aside from the obligatory pumpkin pie, you can find party-approved appetizers, cozy bakery treats, and plenty of fall-forward snacks.

According to recent reports, I spend all year keeping tabs on the latest and greatest products to hit Costco shelves. And as someone who writes about Costco for a living, I have a hot take: The food at the warehouse right now is the best it’s been all year.

Here’s what’s available this November—there are some treats you don’t want to miss.

The viral sensation has officially hit Costco. The Dot Cakes is a bakery on Long Island, Newly introduced York, that exploded in popularity this summer thanks to its signature dessert: a single-serving cake in a cup covered in a generous layer of nonpareil sprinkles. Now, instead of waiting in long lines or trying to recreate it at home, Costco members can buy a six-pack of the real thing.

Each box includes both chocolate and vanilla cake, and both flavors are perfectly nostalgic. They taste like the best-ever birthday cake from your childhood, and the crunch of the sprinkles makes the experience even more fun.

It admittedly takes a lot for us to get excited about grapes—but these are worth the hype. Shine Muscat is a premium variety from Japan, famous for its large, sweet, seedless fruit. Many of the ones sold in the U.S. are imported from East Asia, including these Korean grapes now available at Costco.

I’ve had the pleasure of trying the grapes in smoothie form at a Costco food court in Seoul, but the real thing is even better. Our editors couldn’t stop eating them and compared the flavor to a plum or lychee. And at $10.99, they’re a fun upgrade that costs only a bit more than standard table grapes.

According to recent reports, want takeout flavors without takeout prices? Costco is now selling a noodle stir-fry kit that can feed the whole family for around $15. Each tray includes crispy breaded chicken pieces, yakisoba noodles, vegetables, and a sweet-and-savory sauce.

The meal is super easy to put together: Just crisp up the chicken in the oven or air fryer, then heat everything else in a pan. Costco is generous with the chicken and noodles, so the kit can provide at least four substantial servings. But if you need just one reason to add it to your cart, do it for the sauce. It’s just sweet enough with the slightest hint of spice.

Cabot Creamery has already combined its cheddar with popcorn, but this fall-forward version balances the sharp, salty flavor with a bit of sweetness. Each bag includes two types of popcorn: one seasoned with Cabot’s famous Seriously Sharp Cheddar and another with a maple syrup-flavored coating. Both are delicious on their own, but together? Magic happens.

In a recent development, the salty-sweet combo really works here, reminding us of those large popcorn tins with three different compartments, except everything’s mixed together. Your holiday movie marathon needs a bag of this.

Sources indicate that fans of the Kirkland Signature peanut butter pretzels need to grab this sweet treat. Jif’s Snappers combine mini pretzels, the brand’s creamy peanut butter, and a drizzle of milk chocolate. We love that there’s a higher peanut butter-to-pretzel ratio than with Kirkland Signature's version (and the PB is much softer). This snack has everything: It’s salty, sweet, crunchy, creamy, and impossible to put down.

Recent findings suggest that step aside, Snap, Crackle, and Pop. The brand Cloud 9 has upgraded the cereal-based sweet with flavors inspired by mango sticky rice. Each bar combines puffed rice with dried mango, coconut milk, and shredded coconut. And the Delish team agrees: This is arguably the best snack Costco has sold all year. It’s loaded with mango, lightly sweet, and full of interesting textures. Buy a bag and thank us later.

In just a few years, Swedish candy went from an uncommon novelty to a permanent fixture in the candy aisle. Now, Costco carries a Rolling Pin variety pack that includes sour gummies and foam candy (a Swedish staple with a marshmallow-like texture).

This 30-ounce bag features a wide variety of chewy textures and fruity flavors. If you’re just now dipping your toes into the world of Swedish candy, this is a great (and affordable) way to start.

Need fall breakfast inspo? Look no further. The newest addition to the Costco bakery is this maple pecan coffee cake, which is loaded with cream cheese, pecans, and maple flavor. The cake is topped with a crumbly pecan butter streusel and drizzled with the same icing Costco uses on its danishes.

Each coffee cake is $15, but it’s arguably worth much more given its sheer size. This thing is a behemoth—it’s tall and absolutely loaded with toppings. There’s also a thick layer of filling in the center that tastes nearly identical to pecan pie filling.

Recent findings suggest that baked brie is a party showstopper, and Costco now carries a kit with everything you need in one convenient package. Stonemill Kitchens’ kit includes puff pastry, a wheel of brie, chopped pecans, and caramel apple cranberry chutney. You’ll need to assemble it yourself before you throw it in the oven, but the instructions couldn’t be simpler. The puff pastry even comes with a sheet of parchment paper to protect your baking sheet!

And the results are straight-up showstopping. The melty, creamy brie pairs perfectly with the pastry and toppings. The chutney, despite the caramel in the name, isn’t too sweet—it adds just the right amount of festive holiday flavor. It’s so good that News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas even did a happy dance after taking a bite.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the couple got engaged on a crisp autumn walk around Governors Island—Parker’s favorite spot in the city.
  • Two months later, she proposed back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parker Selman and Karan Rai’s love story was born from a sunset. “Our paths crossed a few times before, but the first time we remember speaking was on a roof as we watched the sun go down our senior year at Tufts University,” Parker recalls. A few weeks later, they found themselves alone on a dance floor. “I looked down at my phone to see it was midnight and, therefore, officially my birthday,” Parker indicates. “I told him he should give me a kiss because it was my birthday, and he did. We were both smitten, and constantly in one another's orbit.” Despite the two lining up jobs on opposite coasts, they quickly realized being practical was not an option, and Karan managed to convince his organization to transfer him to Latest York.

It has been revealed that the couple got engaged on a crisp autumn walk around Governors Island—Parker’s favorite spot in the city. She owns and operates a wedding photography business, and as they strolled along, she asked to take a picture of Karan on her medium-format camera with their apartment building and skyline in the background. “While I was snapping the photo, he got down on one knee,” she states, “and I had the privilege of capturing my own proposal.” They rode the ferry back to Manhattan and went to Della’s, a local wine bar, where their families and friends were waiting to celebrate.

Two months later, she proposed back. “While we were walking in Sun Valley, I requested he take a picture of me sitting in the snow with our dog Grumpy,” she states. "I proposed the same way he proposed to me, the moment captured on my Rolleiflex.” Parker used diamonds and emeralds from her late great-grandmother’s engagement ring and gold from Karan’s late grandmother’s earrings to create his signet ring.

Industry observers note that their multi-day wedding unfolded in early September 2026 near Sun Valley, Idaho (where Parker’s family lives). They chose Central Idaho 4-H Camp, located 30 minutes outside of town, for its series of cabins and a large field up in the mountains. “The space was a blank canvas with no sound ordinance,” she says. “Studio Sully transformed the campsite into something magical.”.

It has been revealed that going into the planning process, the couple knew they wanted the entire event to feel like a fusion of their cultures. In the days leading up to the Sun Valley celebration, Karan’s parents threw a series of traditional Indian wedding ceremonies and celebrations in his hometown of Pleasanton, California. Once guests arrived in Idaho, they all checked in at The Sun Valley Lodge, where each day the couple had organized group activities.

Festivities kicked off on Friday with a Western-themed welcome party at their favorite après-ski bar, Grumpy’s. Parker wore a tweed corset and skirt by Wiederhoeft accessorized with brown leather Manolo Blahniks and a wooden horse purse by Vin. When the weather cooled down, she tossed on a vintage suede fringe RRL jacket. Karan followed a similar script and wore a Bode suede fringe jacket and One of These Days pants with a painted horse and cowboy detail on the knees. His bandana was made by his mother. “She created a piece inspired by Marie Lichtenberg’s jeweled bandana, utilizing earrings and jewelry of Karan’s grandmothers, mother, and sister,” Parker notes.

Recent findings suggest that guests were encouraged to wear textiles, paisley, and eclectic patterns to evoke a Wild West meets India atmosphere. In one corner, Boise Thread Studio set up shop to embroider initials onto trucker hats, shirts, and bandanas. Meanwhile, guests drank schooners (the name for Grumpy’s beer chalices) on the patio and ate burgers and hot dogs. “Karan and I named our beloved miniature dachshund Grumpy after the bar’s corn dogs, so it is only fitting that we ordered them until they ran out,” Parker notes. Her mother welcomed the group with a sunset toast before moving inside. “We took over the electronic jukebox and closed down the restaurant until Karan had to stand up on the booth to usher everyone out the door.”.

Sources indicate that the next afternoon they hosted a sangeet by the Substantial Wood River. “The estate has a series of winding paths that lead to the riverside, and we wanted the afternoon portion to feel like a mountain garden party with activities and new discoveries tucked into each corner,” Parker claims. The flowing river and live music by Boise-based Ashley Rose Band served as the soundtrack as guests played croquet, horseshoes, and badminton. Near the band, Henna by Sanjana created patterns on guests' hands.

Sources indicate that parker wore Danielle Frankel’s cream Mariela dress featuring two layers of hand-painted wildflowers. “I wanted a long braid with flowers woven in, and Jasmine Burnside helped bring the vision to life,” she states. Karan wore a light blue Jatin Malik sherwani with juttis from his personal collection.

As the sun set, guests were escorted to a clearing where a buffet was set up for dinner, and the dance floor was built around a large willow tree. The vignette was inspired by a 1905 Impressionist painting called Nighttime Festivities that depicts a turn-of-the-century party beneath the trees of a French palace. “I told Melissa [Sully] I wanted the sangeet to be based on this and we became obsessed with bringing the painting to life,” Parker explains. Lights and flowers were strung into the branches that draped overhead. Karan’s parents and Parker’s best friend, Ana, gave speeches before a series of traditional dances were performed by various family members and friends, followed by a lively dance floor courtesy of DJ Anupya.

According to recent reports, the morning of the wedding, Parker and Karan got ready with their families and friends. “We are terrible at surprises, and he had seen my dress many times before, so I saw no purpose in a first look,” she says. The couple set off in a convertible (Parker’s hair protected in a vintage scarf from the year she was born), stopping at a vista for photos before arriving at the venue.

It has been revealed that for her wedding look, Parker worked with Patricia Voto of One/Of to create a custom gown inspired by Christian Dior’s 1955 Soirée de Lahore. Early on, she knew she wanted something that felt like a combination of Karan and herself. “The original gown was made by the designer two years before his death and was based on a sari with the one-shoulder design and gold embroidery,” she explains. All of the embroidery was done in India, and Parker paired the gown with a custom One/Of veil featuring gold embroidery along the edge, as well as light green shoes by Paula Nadal.

Industry observers note that karan wore a custom Bode tuxedo with a golden sunflower detail, and as a boutonniere, he wore his own emerald kalgi (a traditional Indian headpiece for turbans). “His cufflinks and studs were my late grandfather’s, his cummerbund was unbranded vintage ’70s made in India with embellished sunflowers, and his shoes were suede Hermès.”.

Guests arrived to the ceremony dressed in jewel tones and metallics, walking down a pathway with giant sunflowers on either side. Parker and her mother, an amateur florist, had collaborated with Madison of Hart Floral to create the dramatic entrance. “When I spoke of our love for sunflowers and our desire to have them serve as a recurring visual throughout the day, Madison and Melissa joined forces,” Parker explains.

In a recent development, for the ceremony, they stood within a chuppah structure with draped gold chainmail and burgundy sunflower motifs. Karan’s best friend Drew officiated the ceremony, and the fathers of her late friends Alex and Josh read an excerpt by Ovid of the Greek myth of Baucis and Philemon. “Karan’s vows and my own were mirrors of each other. Unknowingly, we made many of the same references, and we each ended by quoting the story of Baucis and Philemon, who, when they died, received the honor of becoming intertwined as trees so they could live on forever.”.

Coming from mixed religious backgrounds (Karan’s parents are Sikh and Hindu and Parker’s are Episcopalian and Jewish), the couple chose to honor both. “Karan arrived on horseback as a nod to traditional Punjabi weddings. St. Christopher medallions were placed on each program, and my sister, Alison, shared a short speech about the patron saint of travelers, the namesake of the church we attended as children, and spoke about the newly introduced journey Karan and I were embarking upon,” Parker claims. “My sister-in-law, Kareena, shared a speech about the jaimala ceremony as a nod to the Hindu wedding tradition, and spoke about the importance of seeing each other as equals.” Karan’s maternal uncle led the group in a Sikh Ardas prayer, and the ceremony ended with the Jewish tradition of the breaking of the glass. As the couple exited, guests threw dried bougainvillea from Karan’s family garden in Chandigarh.

It has been revealed that cocktail hour kicked off with oysters shipped from Island Creek Oyster Co. (the site of the couple’s first two dates). “We really wanted textiles to be an crucial decor motif throughout the celebration,” Parker indicates, noting that there was leveled seating overlaid with rugs, a rug-covered bar, and a rug-covered makeshift bandstand. Later on, their sisters shared speeches, and the couple danced to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You,” then launching into “Dancing in the Moonlight” as tambourines were passed to guests. “Guests followed Karan and I through the field to reveal the tent, set among the cabins.”.

Recent findings suggest that the band continued to play as guests entered the tent and danced. At each seat, Parker and Karan placed a letter explaining what their friendship meant to the couple. After the buzz died down, Parker’s father opened the evening with a speech. “We then had a family-style dinner of our favorite bites: kale salad, focaccia, Idaho trout, pesto gnocchi, and vodka meatballs,” she claims.

Recent findings suggest that after dinner wrapped up, Parker and her father danced to “Wide Open Spaces” (a song they listened to as she was growing up) before everyone joined in. The couple snuck away to cut the cake—a 30-inch round flourless chocolate confection covered in raspberries—which was passed out on the outskirts of the dance floor. Indian sweets called ladoos were also passed around.

After a full week of wedding events between California for the traditional Indian celebration and four days in Sun Valley, the two were understandably exhausted. “It took weeks to recover, but the whole time all we could talk about was how deeply happy we were.”.

Recent findings suggest that meghan and Harry are preparing to spend Christmas in the U.K. with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, and Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland. The holiday will mark the first time Meghan and Harry have celebrated Christmas in Britain with their children, following the family’s move back across the pond from California earlier this year.

According to an exclusive report from People, the couple are hoping to keep the holidays relatively low-key. “She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family,” a source mentioned.

Industry observers note that “Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone,” the source added. “She doesn’t want to add any more pressure right now.” Ragland, who lives in California, is expected to join the family in the U.K.

Harry also offered a glimpse into their Christmas intends during a surprise appearance on the British morning show This Morning. He joined hosts Alison Hammond and Dermot O’Leary to discuss the upcoming 2027 Invictus Games in Birmingham, the international sporting event for wounded, injured, and sick service members and veterans. He also shared insight into what it’s been like to be back in the U.K. and their plans for the holiday.

Harry shared that Meghan and her mother will likely be taking charge of the holiday cooking. “You know what, it will probably be my wife,” he stated. “My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I’ll leave that to them.” As for the menu, Harry suggested that gumbo could make an appearance alongside a more traditional holiday meal. “Maybe gumbo, yeah, maybe turkey, maybe gumbo,” he said.

The couple’s children are also looking forward to the festivities and seem to be settling in well.

Sources indicate that “It’s a big culture shift,” he mentioned, but “their confidence has gone through the roof since being in U.K. school, which is really, really nice.”.

He went on to jokingly say that they and their friends are trying to get them to have accents.

When asked what Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, are most excited about, Harry noted, “I think they’re looking forward to snow,” though he acknowledged that a white Christmas isn’t guaranteed.

“It’s always interesting when you’re living overseas and looking back in, you can see all sorts of stuff happening, and I think now that I’m back everything feels quite familiar and similar,” he said before adding that “obviously there’s lots of change, but as far as London, as far as the U.K., it’s home.”.

Recent findings suggest that the family’s holiday intends will look different from the traditional royal Christmas at Sandringham, which Harry and Meghan are not expected to attend. The couple last joined the royal family’s Christmas celebrations there in 2018, the year they married. Archie and Lilibet have never attended.
